note: Reads the Act as establishing an AI auditing ecosystem and flags the weakness of internal-check conformity, which is central to this practice.
title: Conformity Assessments and Post-market Monitoring: A Guide to the Role of Auditing in the Proposed European AI Regulation
explain_beginner: The paper looks at Europe's proposed AI law. It says the law creates two main ways to check high risk AI: providers assess whether they meet rules, and they monitor the system after release. The authors argue this adds up to a Europe wide system for auditing AI, even if the law does not use that term. They warn that letting providers check themselves may be weak. The paper matters because it explains how the law might work in practice and where it needs clearer rules and stronger oversight.
explain_business: For executives, the paper says Europe's proposed AI law would require providers of high risk AI to prove compliance before and after deployment. The authors view this as building a Europe wide AI auditing system. In practice, companies would need checks inside the company and ongoing monitoring, but the paper warns that self assessment alone may not be enough. The key decision is whether to invest early in verifiable evidence, clear documentation, and preparation for stronger safeguards in how institutions oversee compliance. It also suggests watching for amendments that make rules more specific and safeguards stronger, because those changes could affect compliance costs and market access.
explain_practitioner: The authors analyze the proposed European AI Act through an auditing lens. They describe two enforcement mechanisms for high risk AI: compliance checks that providers perform and monitoring plans after market release that document performance over time. They reframe these mechanisms as parts of a Europe wide AI auditing ecosystem. Their first contribution is to use auditing terminology to clarify how providers can demonstrate compliance. Their second is to draw lessons from prior auditing research to improve the regulation. They identify seven areas needing amendment or clarification, especially turning vague concepts into verifiable criteria and strengthening safeguards for checks performed internally.
